parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Explain what is meant by gravitational potential energy and by kinetic energy.

markscheme_points.text: (gravitational potential energy is) the energy/ability to do work of a mass that it has or is stored due to its position/height in a gravitational field
kinetic energy is energy/ability to do work a object/body/mass has due to its speed/velocity/motion/movement

hints: Hint 1: Think about what each type of energy depends on - one depends on where the mass is, the other depends on how it is moving.
Hint 2: Link each one to stored ability to do work: height in a gravitational field for one, speed of motion for the other.
parts.proper_answer: Gravitational potential energy is the energy stored by a mass due to its position or height in a gravitational field. Kinetic energy is the energy possessed by a mass due to its motion or speed.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What stored energy means**
Think of energy as the ability to do work. Potential means stored, ready to be released. Kinetic means active, due to movement.

Step 2: **Apply to the two cases**
For gravitational potential energy, the store comes from being lifted up against gravity. The higher the position in the field, the more stored energy. So $$E_p = mgh$$. For kinetic energy, the store comes from speed. A moving mass can hit something and do work. So $$E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$$.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.part_stem:
A motion sensor is used to measure the velocity of a ball falling vertically towards the ground, as illustrated in Fig. 3.1.

{{figure:figure_3_1}}

Fig. 3.1

The ball passes through points A and B as it falls. The ball has a mass of $1.5\text{ kg}$.

The variation with time $t$ of the velocity $v$ of the ball as it falls from A to B is shown in Fig. 3.2.

{{figure:figure_3_2}}

Fig. 3.2

Use Fig. 3.2 to calculate, for the ball falling from A to B,
hints: Hint 1: On a velocity-time graph, displacement is not the gradient but the area underneath the line between the two times.
Hint 2: Read the starting velocity at A ($t = 0.40\text{ s}$) and the final velocity at B ($t = 0.80\text{ s}$), and find the time interval between them.
Hint 3: Use the area of a trapezium for a straight line: average velocity times time, $s = (u+v)t/2$.
parts.proper_answer: From Fig. 3.2, $u = 3.9\text{ m s}^{-1}$, $v = 7.8\text{ m s}^{-1}$, $t = 0.40\text{ s}$. $s = (u+v)t/2 = (3.9+7.8) \times 0.40/2 = 2.34\text{ m} \approx 2.3\text{ m}$ downwards.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Read the graph values**
My friend, look at Fig. 3.2 together. At A, $t = 0.40\text{ s}$ the line starts at $$v = 3.9\text{ m s}^{-1}$$ At B, $t = 0.80\text{ s}$ the line ends at $$v = 7.8\text{ m s}^{-1}$$ So the time of fall from A to B is $$\Delta t = 0.80 - 0.40 = 0.40\text{ s}$$

Step 2: **Remember area equals displacement**
For any $v$-$t$ graph, area under the line gives displacement. Because the line is straight, the shape is a trapezium. Its area is average velocity multiplied by time: $$s = \frac{(u+v)}{2} \times t$$

Step 3: **Calculate**
Put the numbers in: $$s = \frac{(3.9 + 7.8)}{2} \times 0.40$$ $$s = \frac{11.7}{2} \times 0.40 = 2.34\text{ m}$$ So about $2.3\text{ m}$ downwards.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: On a velocity-time graph, the steepness of the line tells you how quickly velocity is changing.
Hint 2: Pick the same $u$, $v$ and $\Delta t$ as before and use change in velocity divided by time.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link gradient to acceleration**
Acceleration is rate of change of velocity, $$a = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}$$ That is exactly the gradient of a $v$-$t$ graph. Here the line is straight, so acceleration is constant.

Step 2: **Calculate the gradient**
Change in velocity: $$\Delta v = 7.8 - 3.9 = 3.9\text{ m s}^{-1}$$ Time taken: $$\Delta t = 0.40\text{ s}$$ So $$a = \frac{3.9}{0.40} = 9.75 \approx 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$$ This is as expected for free fall under gravity.

parts.label: (b)(iii)
hints: Hint 1: Kinetic energy depends on speed squared, so you need to calculate it separately at A and at B and then subtract.
Hint 2: Recall the mass of the ball and the two velocities you read from the graph for A and B.
Hint 3: Use $E_k = mv^2/2$ for each point, then find final minus initial.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Write the energy change**
Kinetic energy at any speed is $$E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$$ The change from A to B is final minus initial: $$\Delta E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv_B^2 - \frac{1}{2}mv_A^2 = \frac{1}{2}m(v_B^2 - v_A^2)$$

Step 2: **Insert the data**
Mass $m = 1.5\text{ kg}$, $v_A = 3.9\text{ m s}^{-1}$, $v_B = 7.8\text{ m s}^{-1}$: $$\Delta E_k = \frac{1}{2} \times 1.5 \times (7.8^2 - 3.9^2)$$

Step 3: **Evaluate**
$$7.8^2 = 60.84, \quad 3.9^2 = 15.21$$ $$\Delta E_k = 0.75 \times (60.84 - 15.21) = 0.75 \times 45.63 = 34.2\text{ J}$$ So about $34\text{ J}$ increase.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Show that the work done by the gravitational field on the ball in (b) as it moves from A to B is equal to the change in kinetic energy.

markscheme_points.text: work done = force $\times$ distance (moved) or $Fd$ or $Fx$ or $mgh$ or $mgd$ or $mgx$

hints: Hint 1: Work done by a constant force is force times distance moved in the direction of the force - here the force is the weight acting downwards.
Hint 2: Calculate weight times the displacement you found in (b)(i) and compare the number with the kinetic energy change in (b)(iii).
parts.proper_answer: Work done $W = Fs = mgs = 1.5 \times 9.8 \times 2.34 = 34\text{ J}$, which equals the gain in kinetic energy found in (b)(iii).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Work by gravity**
The gravitational force (weight) is $$W_{weight} = mg$$ acting downwards, same direction as the fall. Work done is force times displacement: $$\text{work} = mg \times s$$

Step 2: **Show the equality**
Use $m = 1.5\text{ kg}$, $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$ and $s = 2.34\text{ m}$ from (b)(i): $$\text{work} = 1.5 \times 9.8 \times 2.34 \approx 34\text{ J}$$ This matches the $34\text{ J}$ increase in kinetic energy. The loss of gravitational potential energy has become kinetic energy, with no loss, so work done equals change in $E_k$.
